questions.question: **Select the sentence with the appropriate use of prepositions. **

options.text: They rise with the morning lark and labour till almost dark.
They rise with the morning lark and labour utmost almost dark.
They rise with the morning lark and labour by almost dark.
They rise with the morning lark and labour still almost dark.

questions.solution:
The correct answer is: **They rise with the morning lark and labour till almost dark. **

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

 
• Let us look at the meaning of the given prepositions.
 
 
• **Till**: Up to the point in time or the event mentioned.
 
• **Utmost**: The greatest or most extreme extent or amount.
 
• **By**: Used to identify the agent performing an action.
 
• **Still**: Used to say an action or situation continues to the present because it has not finished.
 
 
 
• The implied meaning of the sentence is: They get up with the morning lark and work until it's almost dark.
 
• So, as per the meaning of the given prepositions "**till**" should be used here.

​Therefore, the correct answer is **option 1.**

questions.question:
**Select the most appropriate idiom that can substitute the italicised words in the given sentence.**

He was sacked from his job because of a *grave error* on his part.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is: **Himalayan blunder**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

 
• '**Grave**' is used as an adjective, 'too'. It can describe something serious, or of great importance.
 
• '**Error**' means a mistake or the state or condition of being wrong in conduct or judgment.
 
• Let us look at the meaning of the given idioms to find out the most appropriate one.
 
 
• **Raining cats and dogs**: A heavy downpour, rain coming down very quickly and hard. (एक भारी मंदी, बारिश बहुत जल्दी और कठिन हो रही है)
 
• **Minding one’s p’s and q’s**: Practice good manners, and be precise and careful in one's behavior and speech. (अच्छे व्यवहार का अभ्यास करें, अपने व्यवहार और वाणी में सटीक और सावधान रहें)
 
• **Picking holes in one’s coat**: To criticize someone by pointing out the flaws in their work. (किसी के कार्य में दोष बताकर उसकी आलोचना करना)
 
• **Himalayan blunder**: A very serious mistake or error. (बहुत गंभीर गलती या त्रुटि)
 
 
 
• Therefore, from the meaning of the aforementioned idioms, it is clear that "Himalayan blunder" is the most appropriate idiom for **"Grave error."**

**​**Hence the correct answer is **option 4**.

**Substituted sentence:** *He was sacked from his job because of a Himalayan blunder on his part.*

questions.question:
**Select the most appropriate collocation to substitute the underlined word in the given sentence.**

The banker warned me not to be __careless from__ my ATM card.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is: **Careless **with 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• Collocation is the combination of words formed when two or more words are often used together in a way that sounds correct.
 
• Let us look at the meaning and use of the given prepositions.
 
 
• From: Used to refer to the place where someone or something starts or originates.
 
• Beside: Next to or at the side of.
 
• With: Used to indicate being together or being involved.
 
• Across: In a position reaching from one side to the other.
 
• On: Moving to a position that is supported by something.
 
 
 
• In the given sentence 'careless' is used as a verb. The verb 'care' is always followed by 'of', 'for', 'with' and 'about'.
 
• "**Care with**" means to be concerned about something very important.
 
• So, according to the options, only '**with**' can be used with '**careless**'.
 
• The implied meaning of the sentence is: The banker cautioned me not to use my ATM card carelessly.

Therefore, the correct answer is option 2.

Complete sentence: *The banker warned me not to be careless with__ my ATM card.*

questions.question:
**Select the most appropriate idiom that can substitute the italicised words in the given sentence.**

I have been a vegetarian for *a very long time*.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is: **Donkey’s years**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• Let us look at the meaning of the given idioms.
 
 
• **Donkey’s years**: A very long time.
 
• **Duck in the thunderstorm**: Looking hopelessly sad and dejected.
 
• **Die in harness**: To die while still working or on duty or before retirement.
 
• **Damocles’ sword**: Any situation threatening imminent harm or disaster.
 
 
 
• So, as per the meaning of the given idioms "**Donkey’s years**" is the most appropriate option.

Therefore, the correct answer is **option 1**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/51867102c7c2f369f6e29d2efe025e3b3367c68261ec20262828d84ca5c8f854.png] **Hinglish__**

 
• The idiomatic expression **"donkey's years" **is used in English to denote a very long time.
 
• The phrase originates from the idea that donkeys live a long time, and also from rhyming slang where **"years" **rhymes with **"donkey ears."**
 
• In Hindi, the closest expression may be **"बहुत समय", **meaning a lot of time, or **"लंबे समय तक", **meaning for a long time.
 
 
• Example: "I haven't seen you in donkey's years!"
 
• This means I haven't seen you for a very long time.
 
 
 
• In Hindi, you might express it like: "मुझे लगता है कि मैंने तुम्हें बहुत समय से नहीं देखा है!"
 
 
• This means I feel I haven't seen you for a very long time.

questions.question:
**Select the most appropriate option that can substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence.**

Every nook and corner __of the house were unclean.__
questions.solution:
The correct answer is: **of the house was unclean **

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The error lies in the subject-verb agreement.
 
• The basic rule states that a singular subject takes a singular verb while a plural subject takes a plural verb.
 
• Replace '**were**' with '**was**' to correct the sentence.
 
• When two or more singular nouns joined by ‘**AND**’ are preceded by ‘**EACH**’ and ‘**EVERY**’ the pronoun must be singular.
 
 
• **For example-** *Every student and every teacher took his or her seat.*
 
 
 
• So, '**was**' should be used here.
 
• The meaning of "**every nook and corner**" is every place: everywhere: every part of the house.

Hence, the correct answer is **option 4**.

**Corrected sentence: ***Every nook and corner of the house was unclean.__*

questions.question:
**Select the correct direct form of the given sentence.**

John said that he was there to resolve that fight for them.

options.text: John says, "I am here to resolve this fight for you.”
John said to me, "You are here to resolve this fight for you.”
John said, "I am here to resolve this fight for you.”
John said, "I was here to resolve this fight for you.”

questions.solution:
The correct answer is: **John said, "I am here to resolve this fight for you.” **

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__** 

 
• The given sentence is an indirect speech and we need to convert it to a direct speech.
 
• When we change an indirect speech to a direct speech, we must follow these rules:
 
 
• The reporting verb "**said**" remains unchanged.
 
• The inverted commas ("...") are placed to show the indirect speech part.
 
• The comma (,) is added after the sentence covered in inverted commas in direct speech.
 
• The first word of the direct speech should be in capital letters.
 
• The past tense "**was**" in the indirect speech changes to the present tense "**am**".
 
• The conjunction "**that**" changes to "**this**" in the direct speech.
 
• The pronoun 'he' and 'them' changed to 'I' and 'you' in direct speech.
 
 

Thus, option 3 is the correct answer.

Hence, the direct speech is - *John said, "I am here to resolve this fight for you.” *

questions.question:
**Select the correct active form of the given sentence.**

The memorial event is expected to be attended by thousands of people.

options.text: Thousands of people was expected to attend the memorial event.
Thousands of people are expected to attending the memorial event.
Thousands of people had expected to attending the memorial event.
Thousands of people are expected to attend the memorial event.

questions.solution:
The correct answer is: **Thousands of people are expected to attend the memorial event. **

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• Most verbs have an active infinitive form, with or without ‘to’
 
• Most verbs also have a Passive Infinitive form which consists of the infinitive ‘be’, with or without ‘to’ + the –ed form of the verb.
 
• The Passive Infinitive is used when the focus is on the receiver of the action of the Verb.
 
• ‘**Be**’ is added after ‘**To**’ and the **3rd **form of the **Verb **is used for making a Passive Voice.
 
• The structure of the passive form: **Object + Is/ Are/ Am + To +Be + Verb (3rd Form) + by + Subject.__**
 
• The structure of the active form: **__Subject + Is/ Are/ Am+ to + Verb (1st Form) + Object.__**
 
• We use the Passive Infinitive For present or future actions happening to the subject.
 
 
• **For example-** My computer is expected to be repaired today.
 
 
 
• Rules of Conversion from Passive to Active Voice:
 
 
• Identify the subject, the verb, and the object.
 
• Change the object into the subject.
 
• Change the verb into the past participle form of the verb.
 
• Change the subject into an object.
 
 

​Therefore, the correct answer is option 4.

Correct Active Voice: *Thousands of people are expected to attend the memorial event. *

• The given sentence is written in the **simple **present tense.

• The simple present tense in the passive voice has the following structure: __Object+ is/am/are+ V3+ by + subject__
 
• Example - 
 
 
• Active voice - *They grow plants.*
 
• Passive voice - *Plants are grown by them.*
 
 
 
• Rules of Conversion from Active to Passive Voice:
 
 
• Identify the subject, the verb, and the object.
 
• Change the subject into an object.
 
• Change the verb into the past participle form.
 
• Change the object into the subject.
